history.name: The ledger audit
history.description: The command ledger audit finds capabilities that shipped without the ledger recording them, such as work done without a coding agent that read the project's instructions. It prints a brief for a coding agent: the range since the last audit, the changed paths grouped into batches, and the commit subjects behind them. An audit covers everything since the last one, or the whole codebase with --full, which is the only way to find a capability the baseline survey missed. The agent records what it finds and then stamps the commit it audited, so the tool knows how much of the repository has not been examined yet. A release with unaudited work behind it cannot be cut, and the refusal says how many commits and files are outstanding. A project that started with ledger bootstrap is already stamped, because the baseline survey counts as a full sweep.
history.dev_notes: src/commands/audit.mjs and src/git.mjs, the only place the package shells out to git. The stamp goes through `ledger audit complete`, never a hand-edit, because it is the one field that makes a gap permanently invisible if it is set without the work being done: it verifies the commit is an ancestor of HEAD, and the brief always carries an explicit --commit so commits landing under a long audit are not silently marked as examined. Every audit is kept in .ledger/audits.json with its mode, so "when did we last sweep the whole thing" stays answerable. The counts recorded there cover backfilled entries only — an audit's current-cycle findings are indistinguishable from ordinary work on the same release, so counting them would mean trusting a number the agent asserts. A reason taken from a commit message rather than from whoever made the decision is marked --reason-inferred and reported by `ledger status` until `ledger audit confirm` clears it, or until someone rewrites the bullet by hand and drops the flag with it. No git, or a shallow clone, degrades to a full sweep with no gate.
